**Finding:** In the depth jumping study — *"Plyometric Training Favors Optimizing Muscle-Tendon Behavior during Depth Jumping"* (Front. Physiol., doi:10.3389/fphys.2017.00016) — **Achilles tendon stiffness increased by 24.5% (p < 0.01)** during depth jumping after the training intervention.

Supporting context from the same study (Muscle-Tendon Behavior Results section):
- The increase in tendon stiffness was accompanied by a shift of **gastrocnemius medialis fascicle behavior toward isometric contraction** during depth jumping — i.e., the tendon took on more of the length change while the muscle fibers stayed closer to constant length.
- **Depth jump height improved** from 31.2 ± 3.4 cm to 36.8 ± 3.9 cm (p < 0.001) after plyometric training.
- Design: 21 young adults completed **12 weeks of plyometric training**, with ultrasound imaging and motion capture during depth jumping.

Note on scope: the other two authorized papers are related but distinct studies — a randomized controlled trial in 36 collegiate sprinters on 8 weeks of drop-jump training (which reported countermovement jump gains of 14.2%, p < 0.001, rather than the 24.5% Achilles stiffness figure) and a youth basketball conditioning study. If you want, I can compare the tendon-stiffness outcomes across those studies.
